description: A council of elders brings together the heads of households or lineages to settle quarrels, share out common land, water or hunting grounds, and agree on joint action. description: Hereditary rank exists when status and leadership pass by descent within particular families, so control of land, herds and surplus is inherited rather than won anew each generation. Archaeologists infer it from burials: at Varna in Bulgaria, graves of about 4600-4200 BCE range from plain pits to a few rich in gold. Whether such wealth was inherited is debated.

description: A chiefdom, in anthropologists' usage, is a regional society of several villages under a paramount chief from a high-ranking lineage. The chief gathers tribute in food and goods, redistributes much of it at feasts, and leads in war and ritual, but rules through kin and allies without a bureaucracy or written law. Tonga in Polynesia is a classic ethnographic case.
uncertainty: 'Chiefdom' is a modern analytical category; whether particular archaeological cultures were chiefdoms, and whether some Polynesian polities (e.g. Hawaii at contact) were already early states, is debated.

description: A mixed-constitution republic has no monarch. Annually elected magistrates, serving in pairs or colleges, hold executive power; a senate of former magistrates guides policy and finance; and citizen assemblies elect officials and pass laws, so that power is shared among the three. uncertainty: The 509 BCE founding date is traditional; the 'mixed constitution' is an ancient theory, and Rome's practice was more oligarchic than the model suggests.
